newsitem.title: UK: Safe-haven demand for US bonds blunted by data.
newsitem.headline: Safe-haven demand for US bonds blunted by data.

text.p: Safe-haven demand for U.S. bonds in the wake of U.S. missile attacks on Iraq will be tempered by the prospect of key economic data later this week, analysts said on Tuesday.
Recent weakness in Treasuries, coupled with analysts expectations that the military strikes will boost President Clinton's standing in the polls, could attract investors.
"There is no shortage of demand at the moment for dollar assets and there is no doubt this addresses Clinton's supposed weakness on foreign policy," said analyst Stephen Hannah.
"But first there is the barrier of the NAPM and the payrolls," said Hannah, head of research at IBJ International.

The U.S. National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) index is scheduled for release at 1400 GMT, and expected to give a reading of 52.9 for August. Figures for August payrolls are due on Friday and are expected to show a rise of 244,000.
Earlier, the United States launched cruise missile strikes on military targets in Iraq in retaliation for Iraqi attacks on Kurds in the north of the country.
Craig Shute, fixed income analyst at Bear Stearns in London, said investors will want to see how the situation develops before committing themselves.
"We've got the traditional safe-haven dash into dollars and that would eventually filter into Treasuries if the situation became more durable," he said.
But some analysts said the threat was growing that a strong NAPM and payroll report would mean the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates when they meet later this month.

"Some people are expecting a rise of 50 basis points, although I think 25 is more likely as (Federal Reserve Chairman Alan) Greenspan favours gradual moves," said Ken Wattret, international economist at Paribas Capital Markets.
"It is hard to imagine that the military situation will be able to turn that nervousness around," he said.
He said the spread between 10-year T-notes and Bunds could widen through 70 basis points to 75 points by the end of the week. It stood at 66 basis points at 1013 GMT.
Analysts said there was also some concern that rising oil prices would add inflationary pressures to world economies, but only a sustained rise would have a major impact.
Rising oil prices lead to higher manufacturing costs, which can in turn be passed on to consumers, thereby stoking inflation and potentially sparking interest rate rises.
It also increases demand for dollars because oil products are internationally traded in the U.S. currency, analysts said.
"A sharp and sustained rise in oil prices would feed through," said Paribas' Wattret. "But we are in a situation, particularly in countries like Italy, where producers cannot pass on price rises."

Shute said the high-yielding European bond markets would hold up well to the threat of increased oil prices. Most European bonds were down on the day, with German September Bund futures off 23 basis points at 97.04 and September BTPs down 25 points at 115.46.
"Dollar strength is putting pressure on the mark, and the better performance of the European currencies against the mark is offsetting the impact of higher oil prices," he said.
Once this week's data are out of the way, analysts said investors will be less nervous of the U.S. market.
"Treasuries are due for a pick up, and with the long bond yield in the seven percent plus area, they will look attractive," said IBJ's Hannah.
